title: Immediate Mode versus Retained Mode
summary: Most user-interface toolkits keep a tree of widget objects that you create once and update. Dear ImGui does the opposite - you describe the whole interface again every frame, as ordinary code, and it draws it. This lesson explains the idea, why it suits tools and debug views so well, and where its limits are.
markdown:
## Two ways to build an interface

**Retained mode** is what Windows Forms, Qt, HTML and Unity's UI Toolkit do. You create objects once - a window, a slider, a label - and the toolkit keeps them. To change what the user sees, you change the objects; to react to the user, you register callbacks:

```cpp-norun
// retained mode (pseudo-code)
auto* slider = new Slider(window, "Speed", 0.0f, 10.0f);
slider->setValue(player.speed);
slider->onChanged([&](float v) { player.speed = v; });   // keep the copy and the real value in sync
```

There are now **two** copies of the speed: `player.speed` and the slider's value. Keeping them in sync is your job, and most UI bugs live in that gap.

**Immediate mode** is what Dear ImGui does. There are no widget objects for you to keep. Every frame, you call functions that describe the interface **as it should be right now**, and each call returns what the user did:

```cpp-norun
// immediate mode: this runs every frame
ImGui::Begin("Player");
ImGui::SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, 0.0f, 10.0f);   // shows player.speed, writes to it if dragged
if (ImGui::Button("Reset")) player.speed = 4.0f;          // true on the frame it was clicked
ImGui::End();
```

The slider reads `player.speed` directly and writes to it directly. There is no second copy, no callback, no "update the UI when the data changes". If the game changes the speed, the slider shows it next frame because it is drawn from the data again.

## Why tools love it

- **Interfaces are just code.** Loops and `if`s produce lists and optional parts: `for (auto& enemy : enemies) ImGui::Text(...)`. When an enemy dies, it disappears from the list with no extra work.
- **Fast to write.** A debug window for a new system is often ten lines, written in the system's own file.
- **Always in sync** with the data, because it is drawn from it.
- **Drops into any engine.** ImGui only produces triangles and textures to draw; a small **back end** feeds them to DirectX, OpenGL, Vulkan or Metal, and passes mouse and keyboard input in.

That is why game studios use it for editors, debug overlays, profilers and in-house tools: those are exactly the interfaces where speed of writing matters more than polish.

## But ImGui does keep some state

"Immediate mode" describes the **API**, not the library's insides. ImGui remembers what it must between frames: window positions and sizes, which tree nodes are open, which widget is being dragged, scroll positions, text being edited. It finds that state by each widget's **ID**, which it computes from the label you pass (lesson 1.05). That is the one rule you have to learn early.

It also means the cost is real: building the UI runs your code every frame. For tools, that is a few hundred microseconds; for a game's main menu shown to players, a retained toolkit or a hand-made UI is often a better fit (lesson 6.03).

## Where immediate mode is not the best choice

- **Player-facing game UI** with animation, art direction and controller navigation everywhere.
- **Large text documents** or anything needing rich text layout.
- **Accessibility**: screen readers and similar tools rely on a widget tree that ImGui does not expose.

For the tools this course builds - inspectors, editors, profilers, consoles - it is excellent.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Copying values into the UI and back
> Pass pointers to the real data. `SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, ...)` needs no copy.

> [!warning] Trying to store widget objects
> There are none to store. If something should appear, call its function this frame; if not, don't.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What is the difference between retained and immediate mode?
- Retained mode redraws every frame; immediate mode only redraws when a value changes
- Retained mode is for 3D scenes; immediate mode is for 2D interfaces
+ Retained mode keeps widget objects you update; immediate mode describes the UI each frame
- Retained mode uses callbacks for input; immediate mode cannot react to input at all
> In immediate mode there are no widget objects for you to keep: each frame's calls read and write your data directly and return what the user did.

? Does Dear ImGui keep any state between frames?
- No, nothing at all; that is what "immediate mode" means
+ Yes: interface state such as window positions and open tree nodes, found by ID
- Only the values of your variables, which it copies into its own widgets
> "Immediate mode" describes the API, not the insides. ImGui keeps interface state (window positions and sizes, open nodes, the active widget, scroll and text editing) looked up by ID, but never a copy of your data.

? Why does immediate mode avoid synchronisation bugs?
- Because ImGui locks your data while the frame is drawn
- Because every widget registers a callback that runs when the data changes
+ Because widgets read and write the program's real data directly every frame, so there is no second copy
> With `SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, ...)` the slider shows and changes `player.speed` itself; there is no widget value to keep in step.

? What does ImGui::Button return?
- A pointer to the button object
+ true on the frame the button was clicked
- The button's ID, so you can look it up later
> Immediate-mode functions return what the user did this frame; there is no button object to keep.

? A value changes in the game. What must you do so an ImGui slider shows the new value?
- Call an update function on the slider
- Register a callback that copies the value into the slider
+ Nothing; the slider is drawn from the value again next frame
> The slider reads the real variable every frame, so there is no copy to keep in sync.

? Which of these is a poor fit for Dear ImGui?
- A debug window listing every enemy
- A property editor in a level editor
+ A heavily styled main menu shown to players with a controller
- An in-game profiler showing frame times
> Tools are its strength; polished, animated, player-facing UI is usually better served by a retained toolkit or a hand-made UI.
```
ideas:
- Look at screenshots of the "Dear ImGui" gallery on its GitHub page: almost every tool you see was written in this style.
- Think of a debug value in a game you have written. Write, on paper, the three lines of ImGui code that would show it and let you change it.
